/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.headline: Healey signals welfare reform push and new apprenticeships scheme
/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.excerpt: John Healey has signalled Labour will stage a fresh attempt at welfare reform as he pledged to put fiscal discipline at the core of next month’s budget, alongside measures to inject hope into Britain’s economy. In his first speech as chancellor to the Labour conference, Healey warned that next month’s highly anticipated tax-and-spending event would need to take into account a challenging global backdrop. Setting out measures to support jobs and growth, the chancellor announced a new local apprenticeship service, to be led by mayors, targeted at young people to deliver “thousands more apprenticeships” across the country. However, he also gave the clearest indication yet that job support would be accompanied by changes to the welfare system designed to incentivise employment while curbing a soaring benefits bill. Rolling the pitch to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion that forced his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, into a costly U-turn, Healey argued Labour had a “moral duty” to overhaul the system to encourage people to find a job. “Our social security system must always be there for those who can never work. But for everyone else, benefits should be a bridge to work, to wider participation, to a better life, not a trap that people can’t escape,” he said. “And, conference, it is simply not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill and a system which offers an income but doesn’t offer a future.
/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.trail: Chancellor sets out measures to support jobs and growth in Labour conference speech but vows fiscal discipline in budget

/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.headline: Severely disabled young people should get fast-track access to benefits, Milburn says
/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.excerpt: Young people whose complex disabilities mean they have little prospect of getting a paid job should get fast-track access to disability benefits, an official review of youth employment will say. The review, by the former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn, will say 16- to 24-year-olds with the most severe lifelong needs should be guaranteed swift and unconditional benefit support rather than having to prove they cannot work. Currently, many disabled youngsters and their families have to endure repeated lengthy, adversarial and often distressing assessments to access personal independence payment (Pip) and universal credit health benefits. The guarantee could include young people with profound and multiple learning disabilities, severe neurological conditions, and those with severe and complex needs who qualify for NHS continuing healthcare support. The review, expected in October, will say there is no need for repeated disability benefits assessments for this group, and young adults should not have to constantly demonstrate proof of lifelong conditions and impairments diagnosed at birth or in early childhood that mean they cannot work. “I’ve heard too many stories of young people with the most severe disabilities left waiting, worrying and fighting for the support they’re entitled to,” Milburn told the Guardian.
/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.trail: Alan Milburn said 16- to 24-year-olds with most complex needs should not have to keep proving they cannot work

/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.headline: Tories target universal credit claimants in plan condemned as ‘fast track to poverty’
/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.excerpt: People claiming universal credit (UC) would have their payments cut by a third if they have not paid enough national insurance, under a Conservative plan condemned by one charity as “a fast track to increased poverty”. Under the proposals, those who receive this “subsistence allowance” would have it paid into a dedicated debit card that would prevent from them buying alcohol or tobacco, based on an Australian system that was scrapped after trials found limited evidence it changed behaviour. While the proposals are billed by the Conservatives as a way to push people into work, the poverty charity Trussell said trimming incomes so that people struggled with rent and transport was likely to make it even harder for them to find and keep a job. Under the plan, UC claimants would receive the full amount to which they are entitled for six months, but after this point the sum would be tied to how long they have worked at a level that triggers national insurance payments. This would have to happen for at least twice as long as the claimant period, meaning someone who has amassed two years of NI payments would qualify for another 12 months of full UC, before falling to the lower rate. Set at 70% of the standard amount, this would leave a single claimant aged under 25 living on £237 a month, or just over £7.50 a day. For a couple aged 25 or over, under the plan they would lose £200 a month, falling to £466 in total.
/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.trail: Proposals aim to push people into work, but charities say families are still paying price of austerity cuts and rise in cost of living

/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.headline: Young people’s Pip claims for ADHD and autism ‘rising fastest in affluent areas’
/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.excerpt: Some of the most affluent areas of England have had the sharpest rises in the proportion of young people claiming disability benefits for ADHD and autism since the pandemic, according to new research. Claims for the personal independence payment (Pip) benefit for these health conditions were typically proportionally far higher in deprived areas with higher rates of poverty, low educational outcomes and insecure employment. However, the fastest growth in ADHD and autism-related Pip claims has been in some of the country’s most prosperous areas such as Wokingham, Warwick, and parts of Hampshire and Surrey. This trend probably reflects swifter access to ADHD and autism diagnoses in more affluent areas, say the researchers, in part highlighting the ability of wealthier families to skip long NHS waiting lists and pay privately for clinical diagnoses. They say the relative gap in Pip claims between rich and poor areas is shrinking, with growth rates in wealthy places such as Runnymede in Surrey outstripping the likes of Blackpool and Stoke-on-Trent. The research also found that Pip claim rates for ADHD and autism were higher among white people than other ethnic groups. This was reflected in lower than expected claims in ethnically diverse areas such as Newham and Brent, in London, and Leicester.
/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.trail: Experts say trend across England probably reflects swifter access to diagnoses as wealthier families go private

/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.headline: ‘Work is good for you’: how UK scheme could help tackle youth mental health crisis
/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.excerpt: Work must be “part of the answer” to the mental health crisis among young people, the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, has said as he met some of the first beneficiaries of Labour’s youth jobs guarantee scheme. He was speaking on a visit to Boots’s headquarters in Nottingham on Wednesday, where several 18- to 21-year-olds were taken on under the job guarantee – with their wages paid by the taxpayer for six months. Some of the recruits were packing and labelling boxes of products to be posted out to households, and others are in administrative roles. They told McFadden about long periods of fruitless jobhunting. “It was just amazing for me to hear their stories,” McFadden said of the recruits. “These are young people who have been out of work for one, two, up to four years. Most of them have been working here for a few weeks. And you can already see how it’s changed their confidence in themselves – their sense of belief in themselves.” A rise in cases of mental illness is widely cited as one cause for the increase in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in recent years. But McFadden said the reasons could run the other way, too. “Work is part of the answer. Work is good for you. It’s bad for your mental health to be sitting at home, isolated. “I see this not only as an economic thing, but as a response to greater instances of mental health problems for young people.
/politics/2026/oct/01/welfare-changes-un.trail: Paid employment can boost confidence and wellbeing, says Pat McFadden as jobs guarantee scheme gets under way

/politics/2026/oct/01/burnhams-reopening.headline: Nigel Farage cries ‘witch-hunt’ – but this may be Reform’s Partygate moment
/politics/2026/oct/01/burnhams-reopening.excerpt: With his personal funding once again under media scrutiny, Nigel Farage, the leader of the rightwing Reform UK party, is adamant he is the victim of an “establishment plot” trying to stop him from reaching Downing Street. This time, Farage is facing questions about support for his lifestyle from the convicted criminal George Cottrell, just months after it was revealed by the Guardian that he also took £5m from the cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne as a personal gift. The accusation that shadowy actors and political opponents within the establishment are against him are being levelled not only by Farage, but by a range of his outriders – from former donor Arron Banks to Reform’s deputy leader, Richard Tice. Andy Wigmore, an associate of Farage from his Brexit campaign days and now on the board of his anti-World Health Organization pressure group, claimed that the news was “[an] old story and irrelevant – Farage was not even elected, not in politics and guess what, the public don’t trust the media witch-hunt against Farage … same playbook against Farage as we witnessed against Trump, didn’t work with Trump won’t work with Farage.” This conspiracy theory – that legitimate journalism investigating a senior politician’s finances is a “plot” or “witch-hunt” – does indeed appear to be straight out of the Donald Trump campaign playbook. Fans of the US president repeatedly made parallel claims in relation to attempts to impeach him during his first presidency.
/politics/2026/oct/01/burnhams-reopening.trail: Media scrutiny of party leader’s finances has undermined his claim to be a politician in tune with typical voters

/politics/2026/oct/01/burnhams-reopening.headline: Celtic nations begin to plan for breakup of UK in event of Reform election win
/politics/2026/oct/01/burnhams-reopening.excerpt: The rise of Nigel Farage has prompted political leaders across Ireland, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales to game the unthinkable: the breakup of the United Kingdom. Unionists who wish to save the union and nationalists who wish to end it are bracing for constitutional turmoil if Reform UK emerges triumphant – with Farage as prime minister or official leader of the opposition – after the next election. Representatives from each side believe a Farage-led government could trigger a hasty referendum on Irish unification and usher in Trump-style anti-immigration crackdowns that alienate the Celtic nations. The possibility of a strong Reform opposition or coalition spooks the nations just as much. It is conceivable that “in just a handful of years’ time, people on the island of Ireland will be looking across the Irish Sea to a country where ICE-like snatch squads are arresting people off the streets” said Mark Drakeford, the former first minister of Wales, referring to the US Immigration ⁠and Customs Enforcement agency. Drakeford, who has repeatedly said he would fight to retain the union, worries that politics in Britain has irrevocably changed and fears there “there may not be time” for a considered debate about the UK’s future if Farage reaches Downing Street or Reform significantly boosts its number of parliamentary seats from the eight it now holds.
/politics/2026/oct/01/burnhams-reopening.trail: Politicians brace for constitutional turmoil if Nigel Farage’s party end up in government – or even as a strong opposition

/world/2026/oct/01/netanyahu-flydubai-ha.headline: Australian couple on plane diverted after flydubai co-pilot’s alleged attack on pilot
/world/2026/oct/01/netanyahu-flydubai-ha.excerpt: Two Australian citizens onboard a flight to Tel Aviv that was diverted after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed the other in an attack are “safe,” the foreign minister confirmed. The passengers are a Jewish couple from Sydney, the Israeli embassy in Australia confirmed to the Guardian on Thursday. No further details were provided. The flydubai aircraft was travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. In a post on social media, Penny Wong thanked the “heroes” for thwarting the attack. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “Relieved to confirm at least two Australians who were on the Flydubai flight to Israel are safe – thanks to the heroes who thwarted the attack and helped bring the passengers to safety,” she wrote. “We’re thinking of those injured and hope for their full recovery.” One of the pilots, whom Israeli officials said was an Omani citizen, is accused of stabbing his fellow pilot. During the alleged attack, the plane plunged about 17,000 feet in just two minutes. Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.
/world/2026/oct/01/netanyahu-flydubai-ha.trail: Two people from Sydney were on board flight to Tel Aviv that was dramatically diverted to Saudi Arabia after one pilot allegedly stabbed the other
